**This is an AI-generated book.** It is being
tested and completely rewritten by hand. Treat every lesson, code example, and
description of sound as draft material until that work is complete.

If you have a correction or suggestion, [submit a pull

The best way I know to find the gaps in my understanding is to explain the
subject to someone else. This book and website are the record of that process:
learning music theory by turning it into Sonic Pi programs, then listening for
where the model and the sound disagree.

Sonic Pi is usually introduced as a way to teach programming through music. That
route has a cost for an experienced programmer. It spends time on loops and
threads while harmony, melody, and rhythm wait offstage. Here the programming is
assumed. Arrays, functions, state, and concurrency become working metaphors for
musical structures.

I began unable to read a note. The 58 lessons follow the order in which I could
make the subject concrete: sound, pitch and time as data, acoustics, pitch
classes, rhythm, intervals, scales, harmony, melody, notation, transcription,
arrangement, chromatic harmony, then four capstones. The representation grows
with the music. A short phrase begins as an array and ends as named voices sharing
a timeline.

## How the lessons work

Each lesson takes one musical idea, encodes it as data, plays it, and asks you to
change a bounded input. Sonic Pi is the laboratory. The programming stays ahead
of the theory, so what you already know carries the load.

Six decisions shape the course:

- **Sound first, name second.** You hear an interval, cadence, or mode before its
  terminology has much authority.
- **Music is data.** A reusable event carries `:note`, `:start`, `:duration`, and
  sometimes `:amp`. Later fields describe articulation, spelling, or provenance.
- **Score and renderer stay separate.** The score records content. A playback
  function interprets it. Changing an instrument should not rewrite the notes.
- **Examples end with musical material.** Test tones establish a fact; phrases,
  grooves, and progressions reveal what the fact does over time.
- **Notation arrives late.** The staff appears in Part 8, once pitch and duration
  are familiar as numbers. It becomes another coordinate system to decode.
- **Ear work runs beside theory.** From Part 2 onward, short drills turn each new
  category into something you must identify without reading the answer.

Ruby idioms receive a short explanation when they first appear. The complete
subset used here is collected in [Ruby for
non-Rubyists](appendix/ruby-for-non-rubyists.qmd). Sonic Pi calls are collected
in the [cheat sheet](appendix/sonic-pi-cheatsheet.qmd). Each *Take it further*
exercise has an entry in the [solutions appendix](appendix/solutions.qmd),
including structural checks for exercises whose musical answer remains open.

This book does not teach instrumental technique. It teaches what musicians are
organising and why, using representations you can inspect, test, revise, and
argue with.

## Working rhythm

Four sessions a week covers the 58-lesson spine in about fifteen weeks, with the
capstones after that. The pattern I use is:

| Session | Length | What |
|---|---|---|
| Two per week | 25 to 35 min | New lessons, in order. |
| One per week | 30 min | Consolidation. Rebuild one recent example from memory. |
| One per week | 30 min | Free play using only the ideas met so far. |
| Most days | 10 min | Ear drills from your own `drills.rb`. |

Every fourth week, add no new theory. Finish a transcription instead. Theory
sticks when a wrong value stops a phrase from sounding like its source.

Run each example in a fresh Sonic Pi buffer unless its comment says that it
continues from above. Read the code before pressing Run. After the first pass,
make the edits under *Change one thing* separately so the audible difference has
one cause. Stop live loops before moving to the next lesson.

## A word on status

The whole manuscript now has a first draft. Every lesson carries `status: draft`.
That means the planned concept, exercise, explanation, and substantive Ruby
example are present. The Ruby has received syntax checking. It does not mean a
human has worked through every example in Sonic Pi or confirmed each listening
claim.

A lesson reaches `tested` only after someone starts cold, follows it in Sonic Pi,
records where it fails, and rewrites from those field notes. Recordings come
after that pass. Until then, treat timing, synth balance, API behaviour, and the
descriptions of sound as claims awaiting audition. The distinction is part of
the method: code can parse while the musical result remains wrong.
